Confucius identified seventy-seven disciples proficient in the six arts, categorizing them by virtue (Yan Yuan, Min Ziqian, Ran Boniu, Zhong Gong), political skill (Ran You, Ji Lu), eloquence (Zaiwo, Zigong), and erudition (Ziyou, Zixia). He noted individual traits: Zhuan Sun was extreme, Zeng Shen slow, Gao Chai stupid, Zhong You rude, and Yan Hui poor. Zigong, rejecting fate, became a successful merchant. Confucius respected figures like Laozi, Zang Boyu, Yan Zhongping, Laolaizi, Zichan, and Meng Gongchuo, and praised others from earlier eras. Yan Hui (Yan Yuan), thirty years younger than Confucius, was praised for virtue, living frugally without changing his joy. Confucius said he restrained himself to conform to etiquette, was not stupid, and shared a philosophy of serving when employed and hiding when not. Yan Hui died prematurely at twenty-nine, causing Confucius great grief. Duke Ai of Lu was told Yan Hui was the best learner, never transferring anger or repeating mistakes.
Min Ziqian, fifteen years younger, was deemed exceptionally filial, avoiding official service. Ran Boniu suffered an incurable disease; Confucius lamented his fate. Zhong Gong, asked about governance, was advised to be courteous and cautious; Confucius deemed him fit for high office despite his humble father. Ran Qiu, twenty-nine years younger, managed military affairs for the Ji family; Confucius encouraged his timidity. Zilu (Zhong You), nine years younger, was bold and straightforward, initially bullying Confucius but later becoming a disciple. Confucius taught him to prioritize righteousness over bravery, and he died in Wei during a rebellion, tying his hat before death.
Zaiwo, eloquent, questioned the three-year mourning period, suggesting one year sufficed; Confucius rebuked him for lacking benevolence. Zaiwo later died in a rebellion in Qi. Zigong, thirty-one years younger, was articulate and wealthy.
Confucius compared him to a vessel and praised his humility. Zigong’s diplomatic mission saved Lu, disrupted Qi, destroyed Wu, strengthened Jin, and enabled Yue’s dominance, altering the balance of power among states.
Ziyou, forty-five years younger, governed Wucheng with music and ritual; Confucius joked about using a “knife to kill a chicken” but later praised him. Zixia, forty-four years younger, discussed the Book of Songs with Confucius, who noted his slight deficiency. After Confucius’s death, Zixia taught in Hexi. Zizhang, forty-eight years younger, learned about gaining office through caution and about achieving success through loyalty and respect. Zeng Shen, forty-six years younger, understood filial piety and wrote the Book of Filial Piety.
Other disciples included Tantai Mieming, initially judged poorly by appearance but later renowned; Mi Zijian, praised as a gentleman; Yuan Xian, who valued poverty over shame; Gongye Chang, married to Confucius’s daughter; Nangong Kuo, praised for morality; and Gao Chai, deemed stupid. Youruo, resembling Confucius, was briefly treated as a teacher but failed to answer questions.
The text lists thirty-five disciples with recorded ages and deeds, and forty-two without, concluding that later accounts vary, with the author relying on The Analects for accuracy.

The king of Nanyue, Wei Tuo (Zhao Tuo), was from Zhending. During the Qin dynasty, after conquering the six states, the Qin annexed Yang Yue, establishing Guilin, Nanhai, and Xiangjun, and resettled criminals there to live with the Yue people for thirteen years. Zhao Tuo served as the magistrate of Longchuan County in Nanhai. In the second year of the Qin dynasty, Ren Xiao, the captain of Nanhai, fell ill. He summoned Zhao Tuo and explained that with Chen Sheng’s rebellion and the Qin’s cruel policies, the Central Plains were in chaos. He noted that Nanhai was remote and could be defended by mountains and sea, and suggested Zhao Tuo could establish a state. Ren Xiao appointed Zhao Tuo as acting captain. After Ren Xiao’s death, Zhao Tuo cut off roads, gathered troops, killed Qin-appointed officials, and replaced them with his cronies. Following the Qin’s fall, he annexed Guilin and Xiangjun and declared himself King Wu of Nanyue. Emperor Gaozu of Han, due to the people’s exhaustion, spared Zhao Tuo. In the eleventh year of Gaozu, he sent Lu Jia to confirm Zhao Tuo as King of Nanyue, with an agreement for envoys and harmony with Baiyue. During Empress Lü’s reign, officials banned ironware trade with Nanyue. Zhao Tuo suspected King Changsha’s influence, declared himself Emperor Wu of Nanyue, and attacked Changsha’s border cities. Empress Lü sent General Zhou Zao to attack, but heat and illness halted the army. After her death, the Han stopped. Zhao Tuo expanded his territory to over 10,000 miles, bribing Minyue, Xiou, and Luoyue, and acted as an emperor.
In the first year of Emperor Wen of Han, the emperor honored Zhao Tuo’s parents’ tomb and his cousins. He sent Lu Jia to rebuke Zhao Tuo for claiming the emperor title. Zhao Tuo apologized, citing fear of King Changsha and the queen’s actions, and claimed he used the title for self-comfort among barbarians. He pledged vassalage to Han, removed imperial trappings, and continued as a vassal. During Emperor Jing’s era, Zhao Tuo outwardly submitted but secretly kept the emperor title. He died in the fourth year of Jianyuan, succeeded by his grandson Zhao Hu. Zhao Hu faced an attack from Minyue’s King Ying. He requested Han intervention, and Emperor Wu sent troops, leading to Ying’s death. Zhao Hu thanked the emperor but, advised by ministers, avoided visiting the capital, fearing captivity.
He died as King Wen. His son Yingqi, who had married a woman from Handan and fathered Zhao Xing, became king. Yingqi hid his grandfather’s emperor seal, refused to visit the capital due to fear of Han laws, and died as King Ming. Zhao Xing succeeded, with his mother as queen mother.
The queen mother, who had previously committed adultery with Anguo Shaoji, sought to submit to Han. Emperor Wu sent Anguo Shaoji to persuade them. The young king and queen mother agreed to become vassals, but Prime Minister Lu Jia, who had served three kings and held great influence, opposed.
He feared losing power and plotted rebellion. At a banquet, the queen mother tried to provoke the Han envoy to kill Lu Jia, but the envoy hesitated. Lu Jia left, gathered troops, and refused to meet the king. The queen mother’s efforts failed.
The emperor sent Han Qianqiu with 2,000 troops to South Vietnam. Lu Jia rebelled, killed the king, queen mother, and Han envoys, and installed Zhao Jiande as king. Han Qianqiu’s army was ambushed and destroyed. The emperor then launched a large-scale attack in the fifth year of Yuanding, with generals Lu Bode, Yang Pu, and others leading forces from multiple directions. In the sixth year, Yang Pu’s troops captured Panyu, and Lu Bode’s forces accepted surrenders. Lu Jia and Zhao Jiande fled by sea but were captured. South Vietnam was pacified, and the Han established nine counties.
The kingdom lasted five generations for ninety-three years. The historian notes that Zhao Tuo’s rise was due to Ren Xiao, and the kingdom’s fall stemmed from internal conflicts and Lu Jia’s actions.

Wei Qing, a native of Pingyang County, was the illegitimate son of Zheng Ji and a concubine of the Pingyang Marquis household. His half-sister Wei Zifu gained favor with Emperor Wu of Han, leading Wei Qing to adopt the surname Wei.
As a youth, he served as a servant and shepherd, enduring mistreatment from his half-brothers. A prisoner once prophesied his future nobility, but Wei Qing dismissed it. He later became a cavalryman for the Pingyang Marquis. When Wei Zifu entered the palace and became pregnant, Empress Chen, jealous, attempted to kill Wei Qing. His friend Gongsun Ao rescued him, and Emperor Wu subsequently appointed Wei Qing as a palace supervisor, elevating his status. Wei Zifu later became empress, and Wei Qing was promoted to Dazhong doctor.
In 129 BCE, Wei Qing led a cavalry attack on the Xiongnu, achieving modest success. Subsequent campaigns saw him capture the Henan region, driving out Xiongnu kings and establishing Shuofang Commandery.
For these victories, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Changping. Further campaigns against the Xiongnu resulted in significant victories, including the capture of King Youxian's forces and vast numbers of livestock.
Emperor Wu granted Wei Qing additional households and enfeoffed his sons as marquises, though Wei Qing humbly declined, crediting the emperor and his officers.
Wei Qing's nephew, Huo Qubing, emerged as a brilliant commander, earning the title of Champion Marquis for his daring raids. Huo Qubing's campaigns were marked by deep penetrations into Xiongnu territory, capturing kings and vast numbers of enemies. He became increasingly favored by the emperor, eventually matching Wei Qing in rank and power. Huo Qubing famously declined a mansion, stating, "The Xiongnu have not yet been eliminated, so I have no intention of considering private matters." However, he was known for his lack of concern for his soldiers' welfare, often discarding food while they starved.
After Huo Qubing's death, Wei Qing's influence waned. Wei Qing died four years later, and his descendants lost their titles due to legal infractions. The text concludes with a list of Wei Qing's and Huo Qubing's subordinates, many of whom became generals or marquises. The historian Sima Qian notes that Wei Qing, despite his nobility, refrained from recruiting scholars, fearing the emperor's displeasure, a principle Huo Qubing also followed.

Sima Ranju, a descendant of Tian Wan, was recommended by Yan Ying to Qi Jinggong during a crisis when Jin and Yan attacked Qi. Despite his humble status, Ranju’s literary and military talents impressed the king, who appointed him general. Ranju requested a trusted minister, Zhuang Jia, to supervise the army. They agreed to meet at the camp gate at noon. Ranju arrived early and set up timing devices, but Zhuang Jia, delayed by farewell feasts, arrived at dusk. Ranju condemned his lateness, citing that a general must forsake family, friendships, and personal safety in war. He executed Zhuang Jia under military law, shocking the army.
When Qi Jinggong’s envoy arrived with a pardon, racing into camp, Ranju declared that generals in the field need not accept all royal orders. He executed the envoy’s servants and horses, parading them before the troops. Ranju then personally cared for soldiers, sharing provisions and tending to the sick. After three days, the army was revitalized. The Jin and Yan forces withdrew upon learning of this discipline, and Qi reclaimed lost territory. Returning in triumph, Ranju was appointed Grand Sima by Qi Jinggong, elevating the Tian family’s status. However, officials Bao, Gao, and Guo slandered him, leading to his dismissal and death from illness. The Tian family later retaliated, killing the Gao and Guo clans. Tian He, a descendant, became King Qi Wei, who imitated Ranju’s methods and incorporated his strategies into the “Sima’s Art of War.” Sima Qian notes that while Ranju’s achievements were for a small state, the “Sima’s Art of War” is profound, and he refrains from further commentary, presenting only this biography.

Lu Buwei, a wealthy merchant from Yangzhai, amassed a fortune through low-cost buying and high-price selling. During the reign of King Zhao of Qin, the crown prince died, and An Guojun was appointed as the new prince. An Guojun had many sons, including Zichu, a middle-ranking son sent as a hostage to Zhao.
Zichu, neglected and impoverished, caught Lu Buwei's attention. Lu Buwei saw him as a rare commodity to be hoarded and offered to help him gain power.
Lu Buwei traveled to Qin to lobby An Guojun and his favored concubine, Mrs. Huayang, who had no son. He persuaded Mrs. Huayang to adopt Zichu as her heir, ensuring her future influence. An Guojun agreed, and Zichu became the designated heir. Lu Buwei gave Zichu funds and married him to a beautiful dancer, Zhao Ji, who bore a son, Ying Zheng.
During a siege of Handan, Zichu escaped to Qin with Lu Buwei's help. After King Zhao's death, An Guojun became king, and Zichu became prince. An Guojun died shortly after, and Zichu ascended as King Zhuang Xiang, appointing Lu Buwei as prime minister. King Zhuang Xiang died three years later, and Ying Zheng became king, with Lu Buwei as regent. Lu Buwei, competing with other lords, hosted 3,000 scholars and compiled the *Lüshi Chunqiu*, a comprehensive text.
He later introduced Lao Ai, a man with a large penis, to the Queen Mother, who had an affair with him. Lao Ai gained power and fathered two sons with her. When discovered, Lao Ai rebelled but was executed. Lu Buwei was implicated, dismissed, and exiled. Fearing further persecution, he committed suicide by drinking poison.

The historian Tai Shigong reflects on Mencius, noting that King Hui of Liang’s focus on profit troubled him, as Confucius rarely discussed profit to prevent resentment. Mencius, a student of Zisi’s disciples, failed to gain favor with King Xuan of Qi or King Hui of Liang, who found his ideals impractical. During an era of reforms—where states like Qin, Chu, Wei, and Qi thrived through figures like Shang Yang, Wu Qi, and Sun Bin—Mencius advocated ancient virtues, which did not align with the prevailing strategies of alliances and warfare. He returned home to compile the *Mencius* with Wan Zhang.
After Mencius, Zou Yan emerged in Qi, observing princes’ decadence and developing theories on yin-yang and the five virtues (metal, wood, water, fire, earth). His writings, such as *The End and the Beginning*, were vast and speculative, tracing history from the present to before heaven and earth formed. He divided the world into nine continents like Chixian Shenzhou, surrounded by seas, and linked dynastic changes to cosmic cycles.
Despite their grandiosity, his ideas emphasized benevolence and frugality, impressing rulers like King Zhao of Yan, who treated him with high respect—unlike Confucius and Mencius, who faced hardship.
Other scholars included Chunyu Kun of Qi, known for his wit and ability to read minds; he remained silent before King Hui of Liang until the king focused on governance, later conversing for three days but declining a prime minister post. Shen Dao, Tian Pian, and Jiezi wrote on Huang-Lao doctrines, while Zou Shi expanded on Zou Yan’s work. The King of Qi honored these scholars with high positions and grand residences to attract talent.
Xunqing of Zhao, at age fifty, lectured in Qi, criticizing Zou Yan’s empty theories and Chunyu Kun’s cleverness. He became the eldest Jixia scholar, serving as Lanling magistrate in Chu after slander in Qi. His student Li Si became Qin’s prime minister. Xunqing condemned chaotic times and was buried in Lanling. Other figures like Gongsun Long, Hui Shi, Li Kui, and Mo Zhai—who advocated defense and cost-saving—also contributed to the era’s diverse philosophies.

Chuilizi, named Ji, was the younger brother of King Hui of Qin, born to a Korean mother. Known for his eloquence and resourcefulness, he was called "the wise man" by the people of Qin. In the eighth year of King Hui's reign, he was granted the title of Yougeng and led an army to attack Quwo in Wei, driving out the inhabitants and annexing the land. In the twenty-fifth year, he captured General Zhuang Bao of Zhao and seized Linyi. The following year, he assisted Wei Zhang in defeating Chu, capturing the Hanzhong area. King Hui granted him the title Chuilizi, with the title Yan Jun.
After King Hui's death, King Wu expelled Zhang Yi and Wei Zhang, appointing Chuilizi and Gan Mao as left and right prime ministers. King Wu sent Gan Mao to attack South Korea, capturing Yiyang, while Chuilizi led a hundred chariots to the Zhou capital. The King of Zhou greeted him respectfully, angering the King of Chu. You Teng persuaded the King of Chu that the Zhou king's actions were precautionary, not disrespectful, and the King of Chu became appeased. Under King Zhao, Chuilizi was even more respected. In the first year of King Zhao's reign, he attacked Pucheng in Weiguo. Hu Yan, on behalf of Pucheng's chief, argued that attacking Pucheng would strengthen Wei and endanger Qin, leading Chuilizi to abandon the siege. Chuilizi later attacked Pishi but withdrew when it did not surrender. He died in the seventh year of King Zhao and was buried east of Zhangtai, south of the Wei River. Before his death, he prophesied that an emperor's palace would flank his tomb, which came true with the construction of Changle and Weiyang Palaces during the Han Dynasty.
Gan Mao, from Xiacai, studied under Mr. Shi Ju and met King Hui through Zhang Yi and Chuilizi. He helped capture Hanzhong and later pacified Shu under King Wu, who appointed him left prime minister. King Wu wished to pass through Sanchuan to see the Zhou capital, so Gan Mao proposed attacking Yiyang. Despite doubts from Chuilizi and Gongsun Shi, Gan Mao captured Yiyang after five months, killing 60,000 enemies. King Wu died after reaching the Zhou capital.

There, Lord Fengyang had died, so Su Qin lobbied Zhao Suhou, emphasizing the importance of diplomatic choices for stability. He proposed a united front of six states against Qin, detailing how each state would support the others if attacked. King Zhao accepted, providing resources for Su Qin to persuade other states.

Fu Zhan, also known as Hui Gong, was a native of Dongwu. He was a descendant of the scholar Fu Sheng. Fu Zhan was a filial and learned man who taught his father's teachings to hundreds of students. During the chaos of the Gengshi era, he served as the Prefect of Pingyuan, where he remained calm, ate coarse grains, and used his salary to relieve the starving people. He beheaded a powerful governor who planned to raise troops, which stabilized the county. When Guangwu came to the throne, Fu Zhan was appointed to high office, eventually becoming the Grand Situ and Marquis of Yangdu. He advised the emperor against personally conquering the rebel Peng Chong, arguing that the emperor should first secure the central territories. The emperor heeded his advice. A thief named Xu Yiqing, who could not be defeated by officers, surrendered specifically to Fu Zhan.
Fu Zhan was later dismissed from his post for a minor fault. He was later recommended for reinstatement but died of heatstroke before he could take office.
Hou Ba, courtesy name Junfang, was from Mi County. He was a serious and dedicated student of the "Guliang Spring and Autumn Annals." As a county magistrate, he killed powerful criminals and arrested bandits, bringing peace to the region. As the Grand Administrator of Huaipei, he was known for his capable governance. When Wang Mang failed, he defended the county. The people begged for him to stay when he was summoned by Gengshi. Under Guangwu, he became a minister and established many good governance laws. He succeeded Fu Zhan as Grand Situ. He was known for being clear-minded and selfless.
After his death, the emperor posthumously named him Marquis Ai of Zixiang, and the people of Linhuai built a temple for him. Song Hong, courtesy name Zhongzi, was from Chang'an. He served under several emperors and Wang Mang. When Chimei entered Chang'an, he attempted suicide by drowning to avoid serving them but was rescued. Under Guangwu, he became Grand Sikong and was known for his honesty, distributing his rent among his clan.
He once recommended Huan Tan to the emperor, but later criticized Huan Tan for playing secular music at court banquets, which Song Hong felt was inappropriate. When the emperor tried to arrange a marriage between Song Hong and his widowed sister, Princess Huyang, Song Hong refused, stating that a friend from humble times should not be forgotten, and a wife from poverty should not be cast aside. He was later dismissed from his post.
Cai Mao, courtesy name Zili, was from Hanoi. He was a renowned Confucian who refused to serve under Wang Mang. He took refuge with Dou Rong. Under Guangwu, he became the Grand Administrator of Guanghan. He wrote a memorial criticizing the illegal behavior of imperial relatives and praising the uprightness of Luoyang's magistrate, Dong Xuan.
He later became Situ and was known for his honesty and frugality. He died in office.
Feng Qin, courtesy name Wei Bo, was from Fanyang. He was tall and capable with arithmetic. He served as a meritorious officer under Yaoqi and was recommended to Guangwu.
He was valued for his skill in negotiating military supplies and was put in charge of examining the fiefs of the princes, a system he established. He later became Situ. The emperor warned him to be a loyal minister, using the example of Zhu Fu. Feng Qin served with respect and conscientiousness. His mother was honored by the emperor. He died in office.
Zhao Xi, courtesy name Boyang, was from Wan. As a youth, he sought revenge for his cousin but delayed the act until his enemies recovered from illness. He was recruited by Gengshi to persuade the Li family of Wucheng to surrender. He fought at Kunyang and was wounded. After Gengshi's failure, he helped friends and Gengshi's family escape, protecting them from bandits. He was falsely accused of conspiracy but was cleared by the emperor.
He served as a county magistrate and governor, suppressing bandits and punishing the powerful. He was known for his mercy, moving surrendered bandits to other counties. He became Taiwei and managed frontier affairs, ordering immigrants to return to their original lands. He presided over the funeral of Emperor Guangwu and established proper court etiquette for the princes. He died at age eighty-four.
Mou Rong, courtesy name Ziyou, was from Beihai. He was a professor of the "Great Xia Hou Shangshu." As a county magistrate, he had no jail cases. He served in various high offices, including Sili Xiaowei, Dahonglu, and Chief Agricultural Officer.
He was well-versed in classics and had great talent for discussion. He became Taiwei under Emperor Suzong and died in office. Wei Biao, courtesy name Mengda, was from Pingling. He was a descendant of the prime minister Wei Xian.
He was known for his filial piety, mourning his parents for three years. He was a learned Confucian who lived in poverty. He was summoned by Emperor Xianzong and became the Prefect of Wei County. He later served as Da Honglu.
He submitted a memorial arguing that the selection of officials should prioritize filial piety and conduct over talent. He also advised the emperor to reduce harsh punishments and select officials with experience as state governors.
He was known for his frugality and charity, leaving his family with no money. He wrote a twelve-chapter work titled "Wei Qingzi.".

The transmission and scholarly traditions of classical Chinese texts, particularly the *Shi* (Poetry) and other classics, during the Han dynasty. The *Shi* of Lu, Qi, and Han schools each had established doctors, while the *Mao Shi* did not. The biographies of several scholars follow, detailing their studies, teachings, and official careers.
Gao Xu, from Pingyuan, studied the *Lu Shi* and served as a doctor, but feigned blindness to avoid serving Wang Mang.
Under Emperor Guangwu, he held various posts, including Grand Secretary of Agriculture, and died in office.
Bao Xian, from Kuaiji, studied *Lu Shi* and the *Analects* under a doctor. Captured by Red Eyebrow rebels, he was released for chanting scriptures.
He later taught the crown prince, wrote chapters on the *Analects*, and held high offices, receiving generous rewards from Emperor Xianzong. Wei Ying, from Rencheng, studied *Lu Shi* and taught hundreds of students.
He became a doctor, minister, and later Grand Herald, known for his moral purity and large following. Fu Gong, from Langfu, inherited his uncle Fu An's teachings on *Qi Shi*, served as a county magistrate, and became a doctor. He simplified his uncle's complex chapters and was honored as Sikong. Ren Mo, from Shu, studied *Qi Shi* and gained fame for personally transporting his friend's funeral. Jing Luan, from Guanghan, studied *Qi Shi* and other texts, writing extensively on various classics. Xue Han, from Huaiyang, studied *Han Shi* and was a leading authority on poetry and prophecies, but died in prison. Du Fu, from Wuyang, studied under Xue Han and taught *Han Shi* to many disciples. Zhao Xun, from Jiujiang, studied *Han Shi* and served as a cavalry captain and tutor to princes. Yang Ren, from Ba, studied *Han Shi* and served as a doctor, known for his advice on governance. Zhao Ye, from Kuaiji, studied *Han Shi* under Du Fu and refused official posts.
The text also covers other traditions. Wei Hong, from Donghai, studied *Mao's Poems* and wrote a preface, as well as works on ancient texts. The *Li* (Rites) tradition is traced from Gao Tangsheng through Hou Cang to Dai De, Dai Sheng, and Qing Pu, with three schools establishing doctors. Dong Jun, from Qianwei, studied the *Qing Shi Rites* and was consulted on ritual matters. The *Spring and Autumn Annals* traditions are detailed: the *Gongyang* school had Yan and Jiang families, while the *Zuo* school was transmitted by Jia Yi. Ding Gong studied *Gongyang Yan's Spring and Autumn Annals* and taught thousands of disciples. Zhou Ze, from Beihai, studied the same text and served as a doctor and minister, known for his honesty. Zhong Xing, from Runan, studied under Ding Gong and helped compile chapters for the crown prince. Zhen Yu, from Beihai, studied *Yan's Spring and Autumn Annals* and taught many students. Lou Wang, from Chenliu, studied the same text and became a leading Confucian with over 9,000 students. Cheng Zeng, from Yuzhang, studied *Yan's Spring and Autumn Annals* and wrote extensively. Zhang Xuan, from Hanoi, studied the same text and was admired for his erudition. Li Yu, from Fufeng, studied *Gongyang Chunqiu* and debated at the White Tiger Hall. He Xiu, from Rencheng, wrote a commentary on the *Gongyang* and refuted other interpretations. Fu Qian, from Henan, wrote a commentary on the *Zuo* tradition. Ying Rong, from Chen, studied the *Zuo* tradition and taught many disciples. Xie Gai, from Nanyang, was a famous scholar of the *Zuo* tradition. Xu Shen, from Runan, wrote *Shuowen Jiezi* and *Different Meanings of the Five Classics*. Cai Xuan, from Runan, taught thousands of disciples.
The text concludes with a historian's comment on the flourishing of Confucian studies after Guangwu, noting that despite political turmoil, the teachings of the classics maintained social order and delayed the Han dynasty's fall.

Liu Yan, a descendant of King Lu Gong, served as a local official and later as Nanyang Prefect, Zongzheng, and Taichang. During Emperor Ling's reign, rebellions spread due to weak governors. Liu Yan proposed appointing powerful governors to control regions, a suggestion initially ignored but later adopted after several governors were killed. He was sent to lead Yizhou as shepherd. In Yizhou, he faced a rebellion led by Ma Xiang, who claimed to be the Son of Heaven, but it was suppressed by Jia Long. Liu Yan appointed Zhang Lu, who later seized Hanzhong and killed the prefect. Liu Yan grew arrogant, built imperial carriages, and killed powerful locals, causing resentment.
After losing two sons in a failed plot, he died of illness. His son Liu Zhang succeeded him but lacked authority, leading to internal strife and rebellion. Liu Zhang eventually surrendered to Liu Bei after a siege, and died later.
Yuan Shu, son of Sikong Yuan Feng, was known for chivalry but later changed. He fled to Nanyang after Dong Zhuo's coup and allied with Sun Jian. Conflicts arose with his cousin Yuan Shao over leadership. Yuan Shu declared himself emperor in 197 CE, citing prophecies and his family's lineage.
His rule was marked by extravagance and cruelty, leading to widespread discontent. After defeats by Cao Cao and Lu Bu, his army weakened, and he died in 199 CE, vomiting blood in despair. His family sought refuge with Sun Ce.
Lu Bu, a skilled warrior from Wuyuan, served under Ding Yuan but killed him to join Dong Zhuo. He later killed Dong Zhuo with Wang Yun's persuasion but fled after Li Cui's attack. He allied with various warlords, including Yuan Shu and Liu Bei, but frequently betrayed them. Known for his prowess, he defeated Zhang Yan but alienated allies due to his brutality. He eventually surrendered to Cao Cao after a siege at Xiapi, but was executed along with his generals Chen Gong and Gao Shun. His life was marked by shifting loyalties and ultimate failure.

Wu You, courtesy name Ji Ying, was from Chenliu County. As a child, he advised his father against writing scriptures on bamboo slips while serving as an official in a distant region, warning that such actions might invite suspicion from the court and powerful families, citing historical examples like Ma Yuan and Wang Yang who were falsely accused. His father heeded this advice. After his father's death, Wu You lived in poverty, herding pigs and reciting scriptures, refusing gifts from others. When criticized for this humble work, he continued regardless.
Later recommended as a Xiaolian, Wu You befriended Huang Zhen at a farewell ceremony, despite criticism for his informal behavior. He became known for his integrity. While serving as an official, he helped the impoverished scholar Gongshamu and befriended the young Dai Hong, who later became a renowned Confucian scholar.
As an administrator, Wu You led by example, resolving disputes through moral instruction and personal intervention, which reduced litigation.
He showed leniency in cases like Sun Xing, who stole money to buy clothes for his father, and Guanqiu Chang, who killed a man for insulting his mother. Wu You allowed Guanqiu Chang to be with his wife in prison so she could conceive a child before his execution.
After serving in Jiaodong, Wu You became Prime Minister of Qi. He later argued for Li Gu against Liang Ji's false accusations, angering Liang Ji. He resigned from his final post as Prime Minister of Hejian, returning home to teach until his death at ninety-eight. Yan Du, courtesy name Shujian, was from Nanyang County. He studied under Tang Xidian and Ma Rong, mastering the classics and gaining fame in the capital. After becoming an official, he repaired Gong Sui's tomb and selected his descendants for office. He abandoned his post to attend his teacher's funeral. Emperor Huan appointed him as Yilang, where he worked on writings in Dongguan. He was promoted to Minister and later to Zuo Feng Yi and Jingzhao Yin, governing with tolerance and benevolence, earning praise from the people. When General Liang Ji sent guests to sell bezoars in Jingzhao, Yan Du arrested and killed them, angering Liang Ji. He was dismissed due to illness and returned home to teach.
He wrote a detailed discussion on the relationship between benevolence and filial piety, arguing they share the same origin, with filial piety as the foundation and benevolence as its extension.
He declined recommendations for higher office, preferring his scholarly life. Later imprisoned during the party proscriptions, he died at home in the first year of Yongkang. His image was painted in Qu Yuan Temple. He wrote numerous works and made corrections to the scriptures. Shi Bi, courtesy name Gongqian, was from Chenliu County. He was eager to learn and served as an official. Concerned about the misconduct of Emperor Huan's younger brother, Prince Bohai Kui, Shi Bi secretly wrote to the emperor warning of potential rebellion and urging restraint.
The emperor did not investigate due to family ties. Later, when Kui was convicted of treason, Shi Bi was promoted to Shangshu and became Pingyuan Prime Minister. During the party proscriptions, when other counties reported hundreds of party members, Shi Bi alone reported none.
When pressured by an inspector, he refused to falsely accuse innocent people, stating he would rather die than do so.
The inspector arrested county officials and reported Shi Bi to the court. When the party ban eased, Shi Bi used his salary to atone for over a thousand people.
As an official, he harshly punished the powerful but showed leniency to commoners. As Governor of Hedong, he cut off correspondence from powerful families seeking favors. When Hou Lan sent a letter requesting favors, Shi Bi had the messenger beaten to death. Hou Lan retaliated by forging an edict and having Shi Bi arrested. Wei Xun, a former Xiaolian, disfigured himself to care for Shi Bi in prison. Fellow countrymen bribed Hou Lan to reduce Shi Bi's death sentence to labor reform. After serving his sentence, Shi Bi returned home. He was later recruited as Yilang but was hated by Hou Lan's faction. He became Prime Minister of Pengcheng and died of illness.
Lu Zhi, courtesy name Zigan, was from Zhuo County. He studied under Ma Rong alongside Zheng Xuan, mastering ancient and modern learning. He was known for his resolute character and integrity. When Dou Wu was about to be enfeoffed, Lu Zhi wrote advising him to decline the reward and preserve his reputation, but Dou Wu ignored him. Lu Zhi refused multiple calls to office until he was recruited as a doctor.
As Prefect of Jiujiang, he pacified barbarian rebellions. He wrote "Shangshu Zhangju" and "Exegesis of the Three Body Problems" and requested to establish academic officials for various classics.
When the Yellow Turban rebellion arose, Lu Zhi was appointed General and defeated Zhang Jiao, capturing over ten thousand men. When the city was about to fall, he refused to bribe the imperial envoy Zuo Feng, who falsely reported him. Lu Zhi was recalled and sentenced to death, later reduced.
After the emperor's death, he opposed summoning Dong Zhuo, warning of his dangerous nature. When Dong Zhuo deposed the emperor, Lu Zhi alone protested. Cai Yong interceded to save Lu Zhi's life, but he was removed from office. He fled in disguise and lived in seclusion until his death. On his deathbed, he ordered a simple burial. Cao Cao later honored his memory.
Zhao Qi, courtesy name Bingqing, was from Jingzhao County. He was proficient in classics but despised his wealthy relative Ma Rong. After a severe seven-year illness, he recovered and served as an official.
He hated eunuchs and resigned rather than work with one. When his brother offended a powerful eunuch's relative, Zhao Qi fled, and his family was killed.
He hid in Beihai, selling cakes, where Sun Song recognized him as extraordinary and sheltered him for years. During this time, Zhao Qi wrote twenty-three chapters of "Etun Song.".
After amnesty, he served as Governor of Bingzhou but was dismissed due to party affairs. He was imprisoned for over ten years. Later recruited as Yilang, he was captured by bandits but escaped. He served as an imperial envoy, promoting peace among warring factions. He suggested to Dong Cheng that Liu Biao of Jingzhou could support the court, and Liu Biao sent troops and supplies. Zhao Qi stayed in Jingzhou due to old age and illness. He was appointed Taichang and died at over ninety.
He prepared his own tomb with paintings of historical figures and himself. He wrote "Mencius Chapters" and "Sanfu Juelu.".

He made friends based on shared ambition, regardless of social status, and believed that fate determined life and death.
As an official, he executed any official who accepted bribes. When criticized for his harshness, he cited Confucius's actions as a precedent, stating a gentleman's official career requires loyalty. Zhao Yi refused all subsequent official summons and died at home. He wrote sixteen pieces.

He resented snobbish friends and wrote "On Breaking the Group," which was compared to Confucius's "Spring and Autumn." He also wrote "The Theory of Debian and Tongzhi." He became Chief of Beixin City, where he prioritized teaching over administrative duties, gathering hundreds of disciples.

Tang Tan, courtesy name Zichan, was a native of Nanchang, Yuzhang. He studied the "Jing's Yi", "Han Shi", and "Yan's Spring and Autumn" at Taixue, with a particular interest in astrology of disasters and aliens. Returning home, he taught over a hundred students. In the seventh year of the Yuan Dynasty, when Zhicao grew in the county, Prefect Liu Yu sought his opinion. Tan replied that his relatives were powerful and Yang Dao weak, questioning if it was a good sign, so Liu stopped reporting. In the first year of Yongning, a woman gave birth to four children, and Tan predicted military strength in the capital and disaster within the court. In the fourth year of Yanguang, Sun Cheng raised troops, killed the queen's brother, and established King Jiyin as crown prince, as Tan had divined. In the fifth year of Yongjian, Tan was promoted to Xiaolian and doctor.
When a white rainbow pierced the sun, he wrote three things stating its fault, then abandoned his official post. He wrote twenty-eight chapters called "Tang Zi" and died at home. Gongshamu, courtesy name Wengui, was from Jiaodong, Beihai. Poor and humble, he studied "Han Shi" and "Gongyang Chunqiu", delving into the magic of "He Luo". He lived alone in the built mountains. During a storm, a voice called him repeatedly, but he refused to answer. The caller entered through the window with a strange shape, but Mu recited his sutra as usual, and no other strange thing occurred. Later, he lived in seclusion in Donglai Mountain, teaching students from afar. Wealthy Wang Zhong offered him a million dollars as capital, but Mu declined, saying wealth has its own destiny.
He was promoted to Xiaolian and became prime minister of Zeng County. There, Marquis Liu Chang did many illegal things, abolishing his legitimate son for a concubine. Mu remonstrated, and Liu Chang wept, listened, and corrected his ways. Later promoted to Hongnong Order, when borers ate crops, Mu set up an altar to pray, and after heavy rain, the borers died. In the first year of Yongshou, floods surged, and Mu warned people to move to high ground, sparing the Hongnong people. He later became captain of the vassal state of Liaodong, died in office at sixty-six, and all six sons were famous.
Xu Man, from Pingyu, Runan, inherited his grandfather Xu Jun's divination skills. During Emperor Huan's reign, Prefect Feng Zui saw two red snakes escape when opening his ribbon. Xu Man divined that in three years, Zui would become a border general named Dongming, traveling three thousand miles northeast, and in five years, a general marching south. In the first year of Yanxi, Feng Zui became governor of Liaodong, attacking Xianbei, and in the fifth year, general of chariots and cavalry, attacking Wuling barbarians, as divined. Zhao Yan, from Langyi, had skills. In the third year of Yanxi, thieves killed the captain and captured Langfu County. The court sent Nanyang Zongzi to attack. Zhao Yan explained the method of "Gu Xu", advising to mobilize Wuyang soldiers to attack Guxu. Zongzi reported, and an edict sent Wuyang soldiers. Zhao Yan pushed Dunjia, teaching them to advance at the right time, defeating the traitors in one battle and burning their camps, pacifying Xuzhou and Yanzhou. Fan Zhi Zhang, from Nanzheng, Hanzhong, was learned and versatile, living in seclusion. He traveled to Longxi and was sent by Qiang general Duan Zhen to conquer the Western Qiang. Surrounded by Qiang, Fan advised that there were no Qiang in the southeast corner, so they could escape and later return to win. Duan obeyed and defeated the traitor. Fan was praised as having the knowledge of Zi Shen, Jiao Yanshou, and Dong Zhongshu, and a special edict was issued, but Fan died of illness.
Shan Yang, courtesy name Wuxuan, from Shanyang Hulu, knew heavenly official and arithmetic. He was promoted to Xiaolian, then Taishi Ling and Shizhong, became prefect of Hanzhong, was dismissed, later became a minister, and died in office. In the last years of Xiping, Huanglong appeared in Qiao. Qiao Xuan asked Shan Yang, who said the country would have a king rise up, and in less than fifty years, the dragon would reappear. In the spring of the 25th year of Jian'an, Huanglong appeared again, and in winter, Wei accepted the abdication. Han Shuo, courtesy name Shuru, from Shanyin, Kuaiji, was knowledgeable in the Five Classics and graphs and latitudes. He was promoted as Xiaolian and was a good friend with Yilang Cai Yong. He reported disasters and wrote poems. In the tenth month of the first year of Guanghe, he told Emperor Ling of a solar eclipse on the 30th day, asking officials to prepare, and it happened as he said. In February of the second year of Zhongping, he predicted a disaster in the palace, and that day, a big fire occurred in Nangong. He was promoted to governor of Jiangxia, dismissed due to official business, and died at home at seventy. Dong Fu, courtesy name Mao'an, from Mianzhu, Guanghan, studied prophecy with Yang Hou at Taixue. He taught at home, with students from far away. He was called up ten times by the Zaifu and three times by public transport, but remained ill.
During Emperor Ling's reign, General He Jin recommended him as a servant. Dong Fu privately told Taichang Liu Yan of chaos in the capital and an emperor's spirit in Yizhou. Liu Yan became shepherd of Yizhou, and Dong Fu became captain of the vassal state of Shu County. A year after leaving, the emperor died, and the world was in chaos. Dong Fu died at eighty-two. Later, Liu Bei became emperor in Shu, as Dong Fu said.
Guo Yu, from Luo, Guanghan, studied under Cheng Gao, learning the skills of diagnosing the six subtleties and calculating yin and yang. During Emperor He's reign, he became imperial physician. Once, the emperor asked him to diagnose a favored minister and a woman hiding in a tent. Guo Yu said there was yang on the left and yin on the right, suspecting a strange person. The emperor praised him. Guo Yu was kind-hearted, treating poor servants diligently but sometimes ineffective with nobles.
The emperor asked a noble to wear ragged clothes, and the disease was cured with one injection. Guo Yu explained that nobles had four difficulties: self-decision, lack of care, weak joints, and inactivity, making treatment difficult. He died while serving as imperial physician. Hua Tuo, courtesy name Yuanhua, from Pei State, was proficient in scriptures and knew how to cultivate his nature. He was recommended as Xiaolian but did not take the post. He was skilled in prescriptions and acupuncture, using Mafei San for surgery.
He cured a man with a throat disease by having him drink sour water chestnuts, causing him to vomit a snake. He treated a county governor by making him angry, causing him to vomit black blood and recover. He performed a caesarean section on a patient, who died ten years later. He cured Chen Deng of worms, but the disease relapsed after three years when Hua Tuo died. Cao Cao summoned Hua Tuo for his head wind, and acupuncture relieved it. Hua Tuo asked for leave, claiming his wife was sick, but Cao Cao discovered the lie and imprisoned him. Despite Xun Yu's plea, Cao Cao killed Hua Tuo. Before death, Hua Tuo gave a medical book to the jailer, who refused, so he burned it. Wu Pu and Fan A studied under Hua Tuo. Wu Pu practiced the Wu Qin Xi, living over ninety with good health.
Fan A knew acupuncture, using deep needles effectively. Hua Tuo gave him Lacquer Leaf Qingnian Powder, and Fan A lived over a hundred years.
Xu Deng, from Fujian, was originally a woman who became a husband, good at witchcraft. Zhao Bing, from Dongyang, could serve Yue Fang.
During a military turmoil and epidemic, they met on the Wushang River and shared their magic to cure diseases. Xu Deng banned the stream, stopping water flow; Zhao Bing banned a withered tree, making it sprout. They practiced together, with Zhao Bing treating Xu Deng as teacher. They advocated frugality, using east flowing water for worship and mulberry bark for dried meat. Xu Deng died, and Zhao Bing went eastward to Zhang'an. He used a plane tree trunk to support a pot to cook, surprising the owner but not damaging the house. He crossed a river with an umbrella, passing through turbulent currents. The magistrate of Zhang'an arrested and killed him for sorcery. The people built a temple for him in Yongkang, where no mosquitoes enter.
Fei Changfang, from Runan, served as a city official. An old man selling medicine jumped into a pot, and Changfang saw this. The old man took him into the pot, where there was a jade hall with fine wine. The old man, a god punished for a mistake, asked Changfang to go with him. Changfang feared his family would worry, so the old man cut a bamboo stick, hung it behind the house, and the family thought Changfang had hanged himself. Changfang followed the old man into the mountains, facing tigers and snakes without fear. The old man asked him to eat feces, but Changfang felt disgusted.

From youth, he possessed noble virtues and profound knowledge, though he disliked detailed textual analysis and was looked down upon by vulgar scholars. During Emperor An's reign, he was recruited as a doctor and later promoted to Tu Chang, but resigned to return home. The famous sages Li Gu and Li Ying respected him as their teacher. He died at sixty-seven in the third year of Jianhe. Li Ying mourned him for three years. Both counties built temples in his honor. Their neighborhood was renamed Gaoyangli after the ancient Gaoyang family's eight talented members. Xun Jing, a virtuous man who refused office, died at fifty and was named Mr. Xuan Xing. In the ninth year of Yanxi, he was recommended as filial and incorruptible, becoming a doctor. In response to an imperial question, he discussed the Han Dynasty's virtue of fire, filial piety, and the importance of proper mourning rites. He also addressed the improper subordination of husbands to wives in marriage rituals, arguing it violated cosmic principles.
He condemned the excessive number of palace women—five to six thousand—which drained the treasury and caused disasters, urging their release to restore harmony. He further criticized ministers who usurped imperial privileges in dress and luxury.
After submitting his memorial, he abandoned his post. Later, due to conflicts with eunuchs, he lived in seclusion for over ten years, writing books and becoming a great Confucian. After the party ban was lifted, he was recruited multiple times but refused. When Yuan Feng died, Xun Shuang mourned him for three years, setting a custom. Yuan An, courtesy name Shaogong, was from Ruyang County in Runan. He inherited his grandfather Yuan Liang's knowledge of the *Book of Changes*. A dignified and authoritative man respected by his state, he began his career as a county magistrate. When a superior asked him to deliver a private letter, Yuan An refused, stating that official business should use official channels and private matters should not seek merit through him. He was later recommended as Xiaolian and served as magistrate of Yinping and Rencheng counties, where officials and people respected him. In the twelfth year of Yongping, when King Liu Ying of Chu conspired to rebel, Yuan An was appointed prefect of Chu County to handle the case.
Thousands were imprisoned due to confessions, and investigators tortured many to death. Yuan An went directly to the prison, tried those without clear evidence, and reported them for release. Despite officials arguing that associates of Liu Ying were equally guilty, Yuan An took full responsibility. The emperor agreed, and over 400 families were freed.
Yuan An later served as Henan Yin for ten years, maintaining strict but fair governance with no bribery cases. He believed officials should aspire to be prime ministers or prefects, not imprison talented people.
He was promoted to imperial servant, then to Sikong and later Situ. When Emperor He ascended as a child, Empress Dowager Dou ruled. Her brother Dou Xian attacked the Xiongnu without provocation.
Yuan An and others repeatedly advised against this costly policy, but their memorials were withheld. Yuan An also impeached Dou Jing for illegally mobilizing border troops. When Dou Xian wanted to appoint a surrendered Xiongnu king as Northern Chanyu, Yuan An argued against it, warning it would empty the treasury and break faith with the Southern Chanyu. Dou Xian proceeded anyway, but the appointee soon rebelled as Yuan An predicted. Yuan An died in the spring of four years, deeply mourned by court officials.
Zhang Youfu, courtesy name Menghou, was from Xiyang, Runan, a descendant of Zhao King Zhang Ao. He studied *Shangshu* from his grandfather and later served Taichang Huanrong, gathering hundreds of followers. During Yongping, he taught *Shangshu* at the imperial school and lectured before the emperor, who appointed him as a minister and tutor to the crown prince. A simple, upright man who strictly adhered to the classics, he was promoted to governor of Dongjun under Suzong. Though a Confucian scholar, he had a strong character and fought against powerful men. He promoted Wang Qing, whose family had shown three generations of loyalty, to a high position.
When the emperor toured Dongjun, he invited Zhang Youfu and his disciples to lecture on *Shangshu*. After fifteen years of service, Zhang Youfu became prefect of Wei County. When Dou Jing sought revenge against Zheng Ju through Zhang Youfu, Zhang Youfu imprisoned Dou Jing's messenger instead. Later, as Henan Yin, he investigated Dou Jing's men who had injured city soldiers and exiled them. After Dou Xian's fall, Zhang Youfu argued that Dou's crimes should be publicly examined rather than secretly punished. He was promoted to Taiwei but repeatedly requested retirement due to illness. The emperor refused, sending gifts and urging him to remain in service.
Zhang Youfu's father lived in the countryside, and Zhang Youfu visited him whenever his position changed. After his father's death, Zhang Youfu was dismissed for scolding an official in court.
He returned home, closed his doors, and refused visitors. Later reinstated as Guang Luxun and then Situ, he died soon after. Before death, he instructed his son to bury him simply without an ancestral hall, using only a straw shelter for offerings. Han Leng, courtesy name Bo Shi, was from Wuyang, Yingchuan, a descendant of Marquis Xiugui.
Orphaned at four, he was known for filial piety and gave away his father's wealth to cousins. As a county official, he secretly handled affairs for a paralyzed prefect for two years. Though imprisoned for this, Emperor Xianzong pardoned him. He was promoted to Shangshu Ling and was known for his talent. Emperor Suzong once gave swords inscribed with names to three ministers, including Han Leng, whose sword was inscribed "Longyuan" for his profound strategies.
When Dou Xian assassinated a marquis, Han Leng insisted the thieves were in the capital, not elsewhere. Though the Empress Dowager was angry, the truth proved him correct.
When officials wanted to bow to Dou Xian and shout "long live," Han Leng sternly rebuked them. After the Dou family fell, Han Leng investigated their accomplices tirelessly, and the emperor rewarded him with cloth.
He became governor of Nanyang, where he exposed villains and maintained strict fairness. Later recalled as a servant, he served as Sikong but died the following year. Zhou Rong, courtesy name Pingsun, was from Shu, Lujiang. During Suzong's reign, he served as an official in Situ Yuan An's house. Yuan An valued him highly, and Zhou Rong drafted Yuan An's arguments against Dou Xian regarding the Northern Chanyu. When Dou Xian's guest threatened Zhou Rong with assassins, Zhou Rong declared he was willing to be harmed to awaken the court. After the Dou family fell, Zhou Rong became famous and rose to Shangshu Ling. As governor of Yingchuan, he violated the law but was demoted rather than imprisoned due to his loyalty. He later served as governor of Shanyang with praise, then retired due to illness and died at home. His son Zhou Xing was recommended for his literary talent and served as Shangshu Lang before dying.

Lang Yi, courtesy name Yaguang, was born in Anqiu, Beihai. His father, Lang Zong, studied the "Jing's Book of Changes," excelled in divination and astrology, and supported himself by fortune-telling. Emperor An summoned him, and his responses set a standard for Confucian scholars. He later became magistrate of Wu County, where he accurately predicted a fire in the capital through divination. The imperial court summoned him with a doctor's title, but Lang Zong, ashamed of being known for fortune-telling, fled by night, hanging his seal in the county court, and never served as an official again. Lang Yi inherited his father's studies, lived in seclusion by the sea, and taught hundreds of disciples. During Emperor Shun's reign, disasters occurred frequently. In the first month of the second year of Yangjia, Lang Yi was summoned to court.
He submitted a memorial attributing disasters to the ruler's governance, urging the emperor to practice frugality, reflect on faults, and reform policies. He warned that luxury, excessive construction, and harsh punishments caused celestial anomalies like prolonged cloudiness, cold spells, and fires. He cited classical texts to argue that the emperor should reduce palace expenditures, release palace maids to restore harmony, and dismiss incompetent officials. He also predicted earthquakes, floods, and invasions if reforms were not enacted.
In a dialogue with the minister, Lang Yi elaborated on seven urgent matters: cemetery fires due to extravagance, hypocritical officials causing yin-yang imbalances, impending droughts and floods, the need to establish an heir, white rainbow portending coups, and the necessity to change the calendar and official titles.
He recommended recruiting virtuous men like Huang Qiong and Li Gu to stabilize the state.
Despite his detailed warnings, Lang Yi resigned from his appointed doctor position and returned home. His predictions of earthquakes, droughts, and barbarian invasions later proved accurate. He was eventually killed by a local knight-errant, Sun Li. Xiang Kai, courtesy name Gongju, was from Xiyin, Pingyuan. During Emperor Huan's reign, eunuchs dominated, punishments were brutal, and disasters were frequent. In the ninth year of Yanxi, Xiang Kai submitted a memorial citing astronomical anomalies—Mars and Venus invading key stars—as warnings against harsh rule and unjust executions.
He criticized the killing of loyal officials like Li Yun and Du Zhong, the neglect of heirs due to excessive palace maids, and the decline of education.
He noted omens like a dead dragon and falling stars, linking them to past dynastic collapses. He urged the emperor to reform punishments, release prisoners, and promote virtue.
Emperor Huan initially ignored Xiang Kai's reports. When summoned, Xiang Kai condemned eunuchs, stating their proliferation caused the lack of an heir. The minister of corrections accused him of slander, but the emperor spared him, citing the astronomical basis of his words. Xiang Kai later refused official posts, including one offered by Grand Tutor Chen Fan, and died at home during the Zhongping period.

Ma Yuan, styled Wenyuan, was a native of Maoling, Fufeng. His ancestor Zhao She was a general of Zhao, and his descendants adopted the surname Ma. During Emperor Wu's reign, the family moved from Handan to Maoling. Ma Yuan's great-grandfather Ma Tong was granted the title of Chonghehou, but his brother was implicated in a rebellion and killed, preventing Ma Yuan's grandfather and father from holding prominent positions. Ma Yuan's three elder brothers were all talented and served as officials worth two thousand shi under Wang Mang. Orphaned at twelve, Ma Yuan was ambitious and unconventional. He left his studies to farm and herd in border counties, eventually amassing great wealth, which he distributed to his brother and friends, living frugally. During the end of Wang Mang's reign, Ma Yuan served as a county official and later fled to the north after releasing a prisoner. He was pardoned and became a successful farmer and herder.
He joined Wei Xiao, who respected him and made him General Suide. Ma Yuan was sent to observe Gongsun Shu in Shu but was unimpressed by his pompous behavior, calling him a "frog in a well." He then went to Luoyang to meet Emperor Guangwu, who received him warmly. Ma Yuan praised the emperor's magnanimity and wisdom, comparing him favorably to Gaozu. He studied under the recluse Zhixun in Nanshan, mastering the classics, and Zhixun married his daughter to him. He annotated many classics, including the "Classic of Filial Piety," "Analects," and "Book of Songs." However, he was criticized for drafting a memorial for Liang Ji to frame Li Gu. Fu Xuan, courtesy name Xiu Yi, was from Niyang in the north. His grandfather Fu Xie was a Han prefect, and his father Fu Qian was a Wei governor. Orphaned and poor in youth, Fu Xuan was erudite, skilled in writing, and knowledgeable in music. He had a strong, upright character and could not tolerate others' faults. After Emperor Zhao's death, when Huo Guang planned to depose the immoral King of Changyi, Yang Chang initially hesitated but was persuaded by his wife to cooperate.
